tether borrows [jj](https://jj-vcs.dev)'s working-copy and operation-log
ideas -- `new REV` to start on top of a commit, the stale-working-copy check,
an op log with `undo` -- and applies them to the state of external systems
that keep their own history. This page is the model in one sitting; the
[Overview](index.qmd#vocabulary) has the eight terms it uses.

## The working copy is the manifests

A dataset is a directory holding `tether.toml` and `.tether/objects/<key>.toml`,
one manifest per registered object. A manifest names the object (`kind` +
`locator`), its policy, and -- once committed -- its recorded `state` and, if
any, its `pin`. Committing a dataset means committing those manifests to the
enclosing git/jj repository. History, branching, bookmarks, workspaces, and
sharing are therefore the VCS's, not tether's. What the VCS cannot see -- what
tether did to the *stores* to get there -- goes in tether's own
[operation log](07-cli.qmd#the-operation-log).

## Commits hold pins; bookmarks hold branches

Two things are versioned, in two places.

A **dataset commit** records, for every object, an exact *state* and -- where
the system can hold one -- a *pin*: a native ref that keeps that state alive.
Nothing about a commit points at anything that moves: not a branch, not
"latest", not a path's current contents. That is what makes
`tether open KEY --rev C` a reproducible read months later, and what `verify`
checks.

A **bookmark** is where writes go. The working copy (`.tether/workspace.toml`,
per checkout, untracked) records which bookmark it works on and, per object,
the branch that stands for it -- its *working ref*:

| Working copy is on | Each Forkable object's working ref | Fingerprinted by `commit`? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the trunk bookmark (`main`) | its upstream branch (`locator.branch`) | yes: the head is what the next commit pins |
| another bookmark, branch created | `tether.ws.<dataset>.<bookmark>` in its system | yes |
| another bookmark, branch not yet created (lazy) | pending: forked from the pin on the first writable `open` | no: until it exists, the object sits at the pin |
| no bookmark | none: read-only | no |

Objects whose system has no branches (files, Delta, DuckLake) have no working
ref on any bookmark: they keep their pin until a trunk `pull` reads them. The
rule: `commit` contacts an object only if this checkout can have moved it;
everything else keeps its pin, the way a file you did not edit stays as the
parent commit had it.

`locator.branch` is the object's *upstream*: what the trunk bookmark stands
for, what `pull` reads, and what `promote` lands on. `--at` is only where a
new object starts.

## State, pin, fork

For each object a backend implements three things, in increasing order of what
the system must support:

- **State**: what the object *is* right now -- an Icechunk `snapshot_id`, a
  Neon `(lsn, commit_xid, branch)`, a Delta `version`, a file's sha256, a
  directory's digest over its files' sha256s. Comparing states is how drift
  is detected without watching anything.
- **Pin**: a durable, GC-proof native reference to a state -- an Icechunk tag,
  a Neon child branch, a git tag, a Lance tag, a Dolt tag -- named
  `tether.<dataset-id>.<hash>`. The hash is content-addressed from
  `(kind, locator identity, state)`, so re-committing an unchanged object is a
  no-op, and the dataset id in front keeps `gc` inside this dataset's
  namespace when several datasets pin one store (see
  [Configuration](08-configuration.qmd#dataset-id)).
- **Fork**: a fresh writable branch created off a pin -- or, for objects with
  `pin = "record"`, straight off the recorded state. `tether new -b NAME`
  decides one per Forkable object, named `tether.ws.<dataset-id>.<bookmark>`
  in each system, and by default creates it lazily on the first writable
  `open`; `--eager` creates them all during `new`.

## Capability tiers

Backends declare capabilities; commands degrade explicitly by tier.

- **Observed** (`FINGERPRINT`): drift detection only. `commit` records the
  state and marks it `recoverable = false`. A local directory by content hash,
  an unversioned S3 prefix.
- **Addressable** (`+ ADDRESSABLE`): the recorded state can be read back later
  with nothing to create or GC. An S3 object in a versioned bucket, a Delta
  version, a DuckLake snapshot.
- **Pinnable** (`+ PIN`): a durable native ref can be created and deleted;
  `verify` and `gc` apply.
- **Forkable** (`+ FORK`): a writable branch can be created off a pin; `new`
  forks and `open` returns a writable handle. Icechunk, Neon, Iceberg, Lance,
  Dolt, git/jj.

Orthogonal flags refine behaviour -- `PROMOTE`, `MERGE`, `DIFF`, `HISTORY`,
`NEEDS_QUIESCENCE`, `BRANCH_IS_STORAGE`, `RETENTION_BOUND`, `CREATE`, ... --
and are listed per backend in [Backends](09-backends.qmd) and defined in
[Writing a Backend](11-extending.qmd#capabilities-decide-behavior).

## Handles, not data

tether is never in the data path. `open` returns a typed handle carrying the
native address -- an Icechunk session on the right branch or tag, a Postgres
URL, a `DeltaTable` at a version, a Dolt revision database -- and
steps aside. You read and write with the system's own library.

## Store writes are plans

Ten commands -- `commit`, `new`, `restore`, `promote`, `gc`, `drop`,
`forget-workspace`, `import`, `repair`, and `upgrade` -- each compute a
read-only *plan*, then *apply* it. `--dry-run` prints the plan, `--plan FILE`
saves it, `--from-plan FILE` applies it later, and apply refuses
(`StalePlanError`) if the world no longer matches what the plan saw. The other
store writes have no preview: `pull`, `undo`, `abandon --gc`, `add --create`,
and the lazy fork the first writable `open` performs.
[Reclaiming Storage](05-reclaiming-storage.qmd#preview-before-you-write-plans)
walks through it; the [CLI Guide](07-cli.qmd#plans) lists every plan verb.

## jj or tether?

Both work on the same repository, so the question comes up constantly. The
rule: **an operation gets a tether command when it has two halves -- one in
the VCS, one in the stores -- that must happen together.** If it only touches
files and history, use jj or git directly. tether notices what it needs to: a
moved working copy makes objects stale, and a vanished dataset commit shows in
`status` and `ops`.

The nouns map one to one. jj's *working copy* is the VCS working directory;
the committed thing is the manifests. A jj *bookmark* stands for one branch
per system: the trunk (`main`) for every object's upstream branch, any other
for `tether.ws.<dataset>.<bookmark>`, forked from the pins where it started.
jj's *snapshot on every command* is tether's **snapshot** on demand: a
concurrent fingerprint of every object on `verify`, `status --snapshot` and
`tether snapshot`, and of this bookmark's branches on `commit`; a plain
`status` shows the last one with its age. A *stale working copy* is a bookmark
whose committed state changed after its branches were forked (see
[Stale working copies](04-branching-and-writing.qmd#stale-working-copies)). A
*detached head* is an object registered `--at` a state: the first commit pins
it, `new -b` forks from it, and a trunk `pull` moves it onto the branch. A
*revision with no bookmark* is a read-only working copy: `open --rev`,
`status` and `verify` work; writes need `new -b NAME`.

The verbs, with the jj command each one borrows from:

| You want to | Use | Because |
| --- | --- | --- |
| record the dataset's state | `tether commit` (jj: `jj commit`) | pins the bookmark's branches in their stores, writes their states into the manifests, commits them, and moves the bookmark |
| start a line of work | `tether new -b NAME [REV]` (jj: `jj new -b`) | creates the bookmark *and* a branch per system named after it, forked on the first write (`--eager`: now) or kept if it already sits at the pin |
| switch to a bookmark | `tether new NAME` (jj: `jj new <bookmark>`) | moves the working copy *and* adopts that bookmark's branches |
| look at another revision without writing | `jj new REV` / `jj edit` / `git switch` | nothing to fork; `status` says the working copy left the bookmark until you `tether new` |
| compare two positions | `tether diff [A] [B]` (jj: `jj diff`) | an object-level manifest diff; `--content` asks each backend for its native diff |
| browse an object's own history | `tether log KEY` (jj: `jj log`) | the system's snapshots, versions or commits; the ids feed `add --at` |
| take what upstream has now | `tether pull` on `main` (jj: `jj git fetch` + rebase) | reads every upstream branch and every branch-less object, and commits what moved onto the bookmark |
| land a bookmark on `main` | `tether promote` (jj: `jj bookmark set main -r feature`) | moves each system's upstream branch -- fast-forward if unchanged since the fork point, native merge where one exists, refuse otherwise -- then the trunk bookmark |
| throw a bookmark away | `tether drop NAME` | drops its commits and the bookmark, then releases its pins and branches |
| reset one object to an older commit's state | `tether restore KEY --from REV` (jj: `jj restore --from REV FILE`) | the branch lives in a store; the manifests and the other branches stay |
| drop dataset commits | `tether abandon REV` (jj: `jj abandon`) | the VCS drops them, descendants keep their manifests as snapshots, and the pins that just freed up are planned for `gc` |
| edit history otherwise: describe, squash, rebase, split | jj / git | manifests are files; nothing in a store changes. Run `tether gc` afterwards if commits disappeared |
| merge two dataset branches | jj / git merge | conflicts are per manifest file; then `tether verify` and `tether new` |
| rename or delete a bookmark | `jj bookmark rename/delete` | `status` then says so: `tether new NAME` continues under the new name (branches fork anew); `gc --prune-bookmarks` releases the old ones |
| push, fetch, review | jj / git | sharing is the VCS's ([Sharing and CI](13-sharing-and-ci.qmd)) |
| open a second checkout | `jj workspace add` / `git worktree add` | the first tether command there starts its own tether workspace; it works on a bookmark of its own, or `--shared` |
| finish with a checkout | `tether forget-workspace` (jj: `jj workspace forget`) | the VCS forgets it and its tether state files go; the bookmark's branches stay |
| check pins; release what history no longer names | `tether verify`, then `tether gc` (after the VCS surgery above) | nothing in jj: pins and branches live in the stores, and `gc` releases what no commit names |
| undo tether's last operation | `tether undo` (jj: `jj undo`; an `ID` from `tether ops` for an older one; run again for several) | the VCS cannot see what tether did to the stores |
| undo any other VCS operation | `jj undo` / the reflog | tether did nothing there; `status` warns if a dataset commit went with it |
| a store lost a pin or branch a manifest names | `tether repair` | manifests are the source of truth |
| publish history as SQL; import the object set from a registry | `tether export` / `publish` / `import` (experimental) | nothing in jj; a derived view of the manifests |

Two habits keep the halves aligned: `tether status` after any VCS operation
that moved the working copy or changed manifests, and `tether new` before
writing again.

### Where tether is not jj

- **Writes need a bookmark.** A store branch is named, mutable, and expensive,
  and must exist before a write can land, so the bookmark is the handle both
  sides share. A working copy on no bookmark is read-only; reads
  (`open --rev`, `status`, `verify`) work on anonymous changes as in jj.
- **`commit` moves the bookmark.** jj bookmarks do not follow commits; a tether
  bookmark must, or its store branches' heads would stop matching the commit
  that names them. It happens in one jj operation, so `jj undo` takes both
  back. `tether commit` also starts nothing new: the next write lands on the
  same branches.
- **Snapshots are on demand.** Reading an object's state is a network
  round-trip, so `status` is local and `status --snapshot`, `verify`, and
  `commit` (for the bookmark's branches) fan out.
- **The stores are remotes.** Pins are what commits reference; bookmark
  branches are local branches; `pull` is fetch; `promote` is the push to
  `main`.

## What tether does not do

- Sit in the data path. `open` hands back the system's native handle and
  steps aside.
- Run between commands. There is no daemon or watcher; every state is
  compared when a command asks.
- Cross-system atomicity. A commit records each object's state within a
  capture window; point-consistency requires quiesced writers.
- Reimplement history, branching, or sharing. That is the VCS's job. tether's
  own `ops` / `undo` / `repair` cover only what tether did to the stores --
  the part the VCS cannot see.
- Queries or transactions across systems.
